claims.text: Conventionally sintered W–Ta–Cr–V–Hf forms a homogeneous BCC matrix.
A post-sintering heat treatment at approximately 900°C for 2 hours in an inert atmosphere will induce coherent nanoprecipitates in W–Ta–Cr–V–Hf.
The heat treatment will produce a uniformly distributed population of nanoprecipitates within the BCC matrix.
The induced nanoprecipitates will be coherent with the BCC matrix.
The coherent nanoprecipitates will act as effective defect-recombination sites.
The nanoprecipitates will interrupt long-range one-dimensional migration of irradiation-induced defects.
Interrupting one-dimensional defect migration will promote localized three-dimensional diffusion.
Localized three-dimensional diffusion will increase recombination of radiation-induced point defects.
Increased point-defect recombination will mitigate irradiation-induced void formation.
Increased point-defect recombination will mitigate irradiation-induced defect-cluster formation.
Under 150 keV heavy-ion irradiation at 800°C, the heat-treated alloy will exhibit at least 50% less radiation-induced void swelling than the untreated baseline.
Under identical irradiation conditions, the heat-treated alloy will maintain or improve tensile ductility relative to the untreated baseline.
The nanoprecipitate intervention will preserve mechanical strength under the specified irradiation conditions.
Untreated W–Ta–Cr–V–Hf typically exhibits more irradiation-induced defect clustering than the proposed heat-treated alloy.
Untreated W–Ta–Cr–V–Hf typically exhibits more irradiation-induced void formation than the proposed heat-treated alloy.
The intervention's effectiveness depends on precise control of nanoprecipitate size and distribution.
The radiation-tolerance benefit may diminish when nanoprecipitate size and distribution are not precisely controlled.
